content.text: Skip to Main content Ancien RegimeIn subject area: Social SciencesThe ancien régime refers to the social and political system in France prior to the French Revolution of 1789, characterized by feudalism and aristocratic privilege. It is often analyzed in relation to the revolutionary changes that followed.AI generated definition based on: International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences, 2001How useful is this definition?Press Enter to select rating, 1 out of 3 starsPress Enter to select rating, 2 out of 3 starsPress Enter to select rating, 3 out of 3 starsAbout this pageAdd to MendeleySet alertChapters and ArticlesYou might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic.ChapterArchival institutions2005, ArchivesAdrian CunninghamThe French Revolution and the nineteenth centuryThe French Revolution provides perhaps the clearest example of the mutable nature and purpose of archives and their tendency to inspire extremes in human emotion. Between 1789 and 1793, much of the archives of the ancien régime were attacked and destroyed by mobs or in state-sponsored bonfires and paper recycling campaigns, with the aim of obliterating what the revolutionaries regarded as symbols of their erstwhile oppression. While such actions might sometimes have had the practical benefit of destroying the evidence of feudal debts and obligations, by and large they were cathartic acts of retribution and ritual cleansing of the body politic.In the midst of this destruction of old archives there co-existed a desire to create new archives, out of which emerged a new archival system for the new society. A legislative repository was provided for by the new Assembly just two weeks after the fall of the Bastille. In September 1790 a law was passed establishing a new National Archives that was to be open to the public and which was to report to the Assembly. By 1794 the desire to destroy the documentary evidence of the Ancien Régime had been replaced by a desire to preserve and manage those records as nationalized public property, reinvented for the purpose of symbolically highlighting the glory of the new Republic in contrast to the sinful decadence and oppression of the old regime. A decree issued in June 1794 granted the National Archives jurisdiction over the records of government agencies, provinces, communes, churches, universities and noble families, thus creating the world’s first centrally controlled national archival system. The same decree also proclaimed the right of public access to these records, thus establishing the first modern instance of archives fulfilling a legal role as protectors of the rights and entitlements of the people and as instruments of accountability and transparency in government The creation of national archives as both symbols of nation building in the midst of turbulent change and ideological − indeed almost mythological − assertions of legitimacy by new orders is a pattern that has been repeated often since. The fate of the archives of the Ancien Régime testify to the fact that no archives can assume an eternal mandate − in the words of Judith Panitch, they are forever ʻsubject to the judgement of the society in which they exist’.23Another aspect of the impact of the French Revolution on archives is worth exploring at this point. Luciana Duranti has argued that the 1794 decree created for the first time a dichotomy between administrative and historical archives − the distinction between the archives of the Republic and the archives of the Ancien Régime. Duranti considers this an unfortunate development in that it represents a usurpation of the administrative and legal functions of archives by social and cultural functions − a usurpation that has echoes in various places and times since the Revolution.24 Other commentators, however, beg to differ. Judith Panitch, for instance, argues that in the 1790s the notion of French archives as sites of ʻhistorical or cultural scholarship had yet to take hold’. While they had acquired the new function of public access for the new purpose of accountability, their essential role as legal, administrative and symbolic institutions remained unaltered.25Nevertheless, Duranti is correct in highlighting the distinction between the administrative/ legal and cultural/historical roles of archives − a source of contestation that shall be explored in more detail later − even if the cultural role of French archives did not become apparent until some decades after the Revolution. Duranti’s portrayal of one role as being innately superior to another is, however, a position that is far more difficult to sustain, as we shall see. Nor, as we have already seen, is it true that the world had to wait until the late eighteenth century to witness an example of an archives that was established for cultural and historical purposes. While such phenomena were indeed unusual, they were not unprecedented − see for example the case of the Han Dynasty Bureau of Historiography referred to above.The creation of a centralized national archives in France provided a model for archival development in a number of other countries such as Finland, Norway, the Netherlands and Belgium during the nineteenth century. Similarly, in Sweden, Denmark and Prussia central archives evolved out of pre-existing royal or administrative repositories. Forty-eight years after the creation of the French national archives, the English followed suit, but for very different reasons and in much less dramatic circumstances. Between 1800 and 1837 a variety of committees and commissions of inquiry had highlighted the scattered and poorly controlled and preserved state of public records in that country. These efforts culminated in the passage of the Public Records Act in 1838 and the eventual establishment of the Public Record Office during the 1850s by a government that was concerned to ensure the proper care and preservation of records that guaranteed the legal rights and entitlements of English people. Lawmakers in Westminster were no doubt aware of the fact that their counterparts in Scotland had beaten not only themselves but also the French in establishing a national archives, when their principal collection of public records had been assembled in Edinburgh’s General Register House as early as 1784.By the middle of the nineteenth century the growth in historical scholarship based on the use of written sources was becoming an important factor in the evolution of European archival institutions. Selected series of historical documents were published, such as the ʻRoll Series’ and the ʻCalendars of State Papers’ in England. In 1869 the Historical Manuscripts Commission was established in the United Kingdom to identify, describe and promote the preservation and use of significant historical records that were not otherwise catered for under the Public Records Act. The Commission, which existed until April 2003 when it was amalgamated with the Public Record Office to form a rebranded National Archives, is probably the best example of a state-sponsored documentation program for the nationally distributed holdings of historically significant private records.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9781876938840500020Book2005, ArchivesAdrian CunninghamChapterLiberalism2012, Encyclopedia of Applied Ethics (Second Edition)D. ConwayEighteenth CenturyThe supreme historical achievement of liberalism, however, has lay less in the development and refinement of any distinctive notions or ideals than in their partial and still incomplete realization. Two historical episodes have been crucial in their advancement. The first was the American Revolution of 1776, when Britain’s North American colonies broke free from British rule to create the United States. The second episode was the French Revolution of 1789. This forever destroyed the elaborate system of absolute monarchy and landed aristocracy known as the ancien régime. In so doing, it helped initiate similarly profound political changes elsewhere in Europe, which by the mid-nineteenth century had seen broadly liberal tenets adopted there, too.View chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B978012373932200226XReference work2012, Encyclopedia of Applied Ethics (Second Edition)D. ValadeTocqueville, Alexis de; born Paris, July 29,1805; died Cannes, April 16,1859; French writer and politician. Born into an aristocratic background, but free of any resentment, he never ceased to examine the revolutionary process which had been set in motion in 1789. A great traveler, an observer of American democracy, and an analyst of the Ancien Régime in France, he was also a deputy under the Second Republic. His name is associated with a contemplation of the origin and future of democratic society, as well as with a method—comparativism—which was applied spontaneously in his two major works, De la Démocratie en Amérique (Democracy in America) (1835–1840), and L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution (The Ancien Régime and the Revolution) (1856), both of which made their author into a central figure in social science.View chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B0080430767003442Reference work2001, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral SciencesB. ValadeChapterFeudalism and Feudal Society2020, International Encyclopedia of Human Geography (Second Edition)Simon ChilversThe Paternity of FeudalismThe first works both appraising the distinctiveness of feudal society and enquiring into its origins were written in The Enlightenment and context of French politics. Le comte de Boulainvilliers argued that Frank warriors of the 5th Century freely chose their war leaders and established the Ancien Régime. As peers, French lords had primordial rights that 18th-Century despots infringed by centralizing power. L'abbé Dubos maintained that the precedent for absolutism was the Roman imperium (a magistracy governed by an official with unlimited power). The Franks had supposedly at first ruled only according to the will of the Gallo-Roman majority. The creation of seigneurial jurisdictions in the 9th and 10th centuries usurped this Romantic power.Montesquieu argued that the Franks conquered the former Roman territories, rather than merely administrating them. In his theory of the ideal distribution of power, monarchs needed to be regulated by lords possessing sufficient independence and counterweight, that is, with seigneurial courts and exempted from taxation. That these customs were lost by the Germanic aristocracy was due to their ignorance of Roman law. Marx, though following Montesquieu on the nature of absolutism, went beyond royal and aristocratic lineages to explain the emergence of feudal society. A short sketch in his Grundrisse offered the first non-genetic theory of feudalism. It held that two anterior modes of production fused together into a new one. Feudalism was the outcome of rural semicommunal tribal life overlaying urban civilization and chattel slavery. The exact way in which the Germanic and Roman precedents related, though, remained unclear.Early 20th-Century scholars, like Bloch and Ganshof, independently collected evidence to support the idea of a union between social orders. Yet when considering the traits of Western European feudal society, what originated from where proved difficult to say. Monarchy could be traced back to either a war leader or magistrate. Both the German comitatus and Roman clientela preceded vassalage. Benefices had an ecclesiastical presence in the Roman world, but some allocations of tribal land were not dissimilar. Serfdom possibly came from either the imperial colonus or “commendation” of tribesmen to serve warriors. The manor was portended only by the Roman villa, with the village a Germanic institution.In Victorian England, whether Normans or Anglo-Saxons contributed more to national identity framed the discussions of feudalism. J. H. Round and Edward A. Freeman respectively defended Norman/Roman and Anglo-Saxon/Germanic positions. Later scholars, including Postan, felt that the Romans established a template for society, though F. M. Stenton's work showed the Scandinavian invasions of later centuries left much of the country under Dane law. Vinogradoff, earlier tracing the origins of the manor, remarked on the priority of Celtic taeogs (non-kin) and quasicommunal land use. For him, the Romans permitted tribal autonomy, with native arrangements informing villeinage and open fields.The completeness of the transition from tribalism and slavery was questioned by D. D. Kosambi in the 1950s. Describing the subcontinent, the “reciprocal interaction” of Europe occurred, but elements were more rearranged than merged. He argued that prehistoric society influenced the form of slave empires, like the Mauryan, with various practices carried over into feudalism. Changing agricultural techniques and the growth of religious houses were linked, with both slave and feudal society needing to ideologically incorporate feminine motifs into a new and largely masculine suture. Serfdom never existed, for there were no Romanesque manorial antecedent. The equivalent of demesne cultivation was undertaken by slaves.Bois made a similar claim to Kosambi, but for Normandy in the year 1000. Serfs were slaves, for there was an unlimited right to their labor–power, with lords giving nothing in return. As during antiquity, serfs were chattel. Claude Meillassoux offered another perspective, emphasizing relations of reproduction over those of production and—rejecting the mode of production concept—focusing upon modes of exploitation. He argued that the economic dissolution of slavery created feudalism. Slavery was unprofitable when capturing laborers from other reproductive communities became impossible, leading to slave breeding and then quasiautonomous homesteads. Unlike the legal emphasis of Bois, slavery involved a rent bound up with the theft of labor–power from another reproductive community. Serfs were neither captured nor bought, but reproduced themselves, using part of their surplus to raise the next generation. Serfdom was therefore less lucrative and homesteads gave serfs a basis for resistance.Like Meillassoux, Barry Hindess, writing with Hirst, distinguished between mode of exploitation and mode of production. However, they considered the latter concept to be invaluable. The problem with Marx's account of precapitalist modes of production was that feudal rent did not represent something economic. Political-ideological forms were predominate, for laborers did not get exploited in the economic instance, that is, during the production process. An elaboration of this view by Étienne Balibar influenced Brenner and Anderson. Trying to reconcile the idea of a feudal mode of production with Marx's base/superstructure thesis, Balibar construed the political-ideological instance to be dominant, though determined by the economy in the last instance. For Hindess and Hirst, it reduced economic relations to Marx's truism that the Middle Ages did not live off Catholicism alone.Hindess and Hirst held that it was through the organization of feudal property that exploitation occurred. Marx concentrated on how serfs were subordinate, not that lords possessed title. With land hunger and no allodium (unowned land), lords had rights of both exclusion and to dictate how rent was paid. Title allowed them to control the relationship of tenants to the means of production and reproduction. Lords determined the size and character of land used—making the reproduction of the means of production also a reproduction of the relationships of production. Laborers set the means of production in motion, but they exercised power neither over everything necessary for production nor reproduction, besides only having what capacity they did within their tenure period and its terms.The distinctiveness of feudal society due to struggles over the control of reproduction became linked to patriarchy and the transition debate by Silvia Federici in the 2000s. Women's history represented class history and capitalism a “counter-revolution” to powerful laborer struggles against feudal rent, the opposite of Brenner's view. Primitive accumulation included stripping women of their control over the means of production and reproduction in both an economic and biological sense. Witch hunts and rape were major techniques of discipline. Nevertheless, Federici saw women to be generally better off in feudal society, for a greater community of support existed. Furthermore, lords attenuated how husbands related to wives. By governing access to land, lords partially regulated marriage and procreation.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081022955104627Reference work2020, International Encyclopedia of Human Geography (Second Edition)Simon ChilversChapterFeudalism2015, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (Second Edition)Levi RoachThe Legal Model: Feudal Tenure and the ‘Feudo-Vassalic Contract’The pioneering work on feudalism was undertaken in eighteenth-century France. Within this context, the term (French: féodalité) was used to characterize the tenurial structure of the Ancien régime; feudalism was seen as the system of land holding, which evolved during in the Middle Ages. This legal-tenurial model of feudalism continues to be employed by historians and is sometimes termed feudalism in the ‘strict’ sense, since its places a strong emphasis on fief-holding as its defining characteristic (see Ganshof, 1961: pp. xv–xviii). In some languages this model is even distinguished from its other socioeconomic counterparts. Thus in German Lehnswesen denotes feudalism in a legal sense, while Feudalismus is preferred for other models, and in Dutch a similar distinction is made between leenstelsel and feodalisme.According to the legal model, feudalism is characterized above all by feudal tenure: it is a system of land holding based on fiefs or benefices (beneficia (singular: beneficium): the latter term predominates in sources before the eleventh century), a form of conditional tenure, generally for one or more lifetimes. For tenure to qualify as truly feudal, however, the tenant must not only hold his land as a fief or benefice, but also be the vassal of his landlord. Thus feudalism combines a tenurial agreement with a social bond (in the technical language of feudal law these are referred to as ‘enfeoffment’ and ‘vassalage’ respectively). Traditional teaching holds that enfeoffment and vassalage were originally distinct, but came to be associated in the course of the seventh and eighth centuries, when the powerful Carolingian dynasty came to prominence in mainland Europe. This period saw much infighting within Francia (a region encompassing much of modern France as well as parts of Germany, the Low Countries, Switzerland, Austria, and northern Spain) as well as the rapid expansion of the Frankish realm from 751 onward. As a consequence – so the traditional wisdom – vassalage and fief-holding became associated: in order to attract ever larger numbers of warriors, the Carolingian rulers rewarded their followers with temporary landholdings in the form of benefices (generally taken from the Church). The result was that benefice-holding (or enfeoffment, as it would later be known) became related closely with vassalic status, eventually leading to the unification of the two phenomena (Ganshof, 1961: pp. 16–50, esp. 16–19; Mitteis 1933: pp. 521–524). This ‘union of fief and vassalage’, of a tenurial agreement and a personal bond of lordship, was the foundation of European feudalism. Although this first emerged in the Frankish heartlands, it was soon exported across the rest of Western Europe by means of conquest and settlement.This form of tenure in exchange for service was defined by two rituals, homage and investiture, relating respectively to the two elements of the feudal relationship (the personal and the tenurial). The first forged the bond of service: by placing his hands within those of his lord and swearing fealty a man became a vassal. The second, which generally followed on from the first, enacted the property transaction: by handing over objects symbolizing tenure and service (often swords, spears, or banners), the lord invested his vassal in his fief or benefice. Together these acts created the so-called feudo-vassalic contract (Mitteis, 1933: pp. 481–518; Ganshof, 1961: pp. 70–72 and 133–142; Le Goff, 1980). There were important consequences of this for both sides: henceforth the lord could expect loyalty and service – the ‘advice and assistance’ (consilium et auxilium) mentioned in many contemporary texts – from his man; the vassal, on the other hand, could anticipate receiving support and protection from his lord. In theory, if either party failed in its obligations, then the contract was dissolved and the property reverted to the lord. The contract also came to an end upon the death of either party. In the early days of feudalism, the lord might then enfeoff a new vassal; however, fiefs had a tendency to become inheritable and from the late ninth century what tended to happen was that homage and investiture would be repeated whenever lord or man died (what in German is termed Herrenfall and Mannfall). In this manner the fiction of the fief's reversion to the lord was retained, while the rights of the vassal's heirs to inherit were respected. In some parts of Europe heirs also had to pay a special due in order to inherit (a ‘feudal relief’); nevertheless, the expectation of inheritance was generally strong (Mitteis 1933: esp. 135–146; Ganshof, 1961: esp. 133–139; cf Bonnassie, 1991: pp. 172–174).The strength of this model of feudalism lies in its precision: it is possible to test for the presence of fiefs and vassalage empirically. Its greatest danger, however, lies in its prescriptiveness. The scholars responsible for it, above all the Belgian historian François Louis Ganshof and his German counterpart Heinrich Mitteis, tended to see feudal tenure in very legalistic terms. As a consequence, they frequently imposed modern tenurial and legal clarity onto affairs which were less formalized (indeed, in their work both scholars were forced to acknowledge many ‘anomalies’ and ‘regional variations’). More problematic, however, is the premise on which this model rests: namely, that benefice-holding and vassalic status coalesced in the eighth and ninth centuries. As we shall see, there is good reason to doubt that this took place (at least so early). Rejecting such an early unification of fief and vassalage has significant implications. Whereas Ganshof and Mitteis treated feudalism as an early medieval phenomenon, treating the development of rights of inheritance and the multiplication of vassalic bonds as signs of the weakening of this system in the central Middle Ages, it now seems that these latter phenomena an integral part of feudalism from the start. As a consequence historians increasingly see the central and later Middle Ages as the heyday of feudal tenure, rather than as a period of decadence and decline (Carpenter, 2000; Spieβ, 2009, 2013).Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780080970868620056Reference work2015, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (Second Edition)Levi RoachChapterParliaments, History of2001, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral SciencesE.C. de Rezende Martins2 OriginsModern parliaments stem from two roots. The first of these is the corporative assemblies of the Estates that were summoned under the Ancien Regime in Europe, and the second, the broad-based popular representation originating from revolutionary movements. The first model of corporative representation brought together the three Estates—namely, the nobility, the clergy, and the ‘third estate’ which evolved gradually into a form of parliamentary representation as sovereign rulers required assent to levy taxes and make war. This first version of the dependence of the sovereign ruler on an institution of a parliamentary nature did not lead directly to democracy nor to recognition of popular sovereignty. The origin of these lies in the second root of modern parliaments—the popular revolutionary root—from which stem: the origins of the process of definition of popular sovereignty, the concept of citizenship, the legitimacy of power based on representation and the delegation of sovereign power, the rule of impersonality of the law within a context of absolute civil equality among citizens, the extension of such rights to all adult citizens within society and the adoption and consolidation of liberal democracy, the expansion of suffrage and political parties, the constitution of government and of its control (under both the parliamentary and presidential systems), and the expression of popular will through the ballot. Both roots reflect anti-absolutist sentiments and it is from them that a representative democratic model, with elections at predetermined intervals, developed.Both these origins of parliamentary power are clearly preserved and apparent in the structure and functioning of the British parliament. The House of Commons, based upon the weight it amassed in the civil war of 1642–9 and the upon manifestation of its social powers in the Glorious Revolution of 1688–9, assumed its role of expressing the collective will as a source of power detrimental to that of the Crown. The result of the revolution, which established the right of parliament to chose a new sovereign, is reflected in the jusnaturalist and contractual arguments presented in Locke's Two Treaties on Civil Government (1690)—one of the principal theoretical works in support of the legitimacy and controlling powers of parliament.The House of Lords, with its elitist composition, preserves the corporativist tradition of the Estates. Modern French tradition, established with the Jeu de Paume Oath of June 20,1789 at the advent of the French Revolution, signals a break with the system of Estates General of the Ancien Regime and use of the term Parliament to designate the judicial and notarial functions, as it had since the twelfth century. The parliamentary assembly installed in the very earliest days of the revolution enshrined the principal of popular sovereignty. In both the British and the French cases, affirmation of the principle of popular sovereignty arose from revolutionary movements, whereby the political absolutism of European states was substituted by constitutionalism. The role performed by a representative system in the formation of the United States is unique. The affirmation of the will of the Americans against unconditional rule by the British Crown led to the establishment of a community-based version of the decision-making process, similar to the community practices of the Protestant congregations, which served as a collegiate political model for the provincial and continental congresses, in which no form of corporative representation was present.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B0080430767027455Reference work2001, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral SciencesE.C. de Rezende MartinsChapterConsumption, History of2015, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (Second Edition)Emanuela ScarpelliniIntellectual Background and TheoriesAs stated above, the history of consumption has encouraged the adoption of an interdisciplinary viewpoint, involving a variety of theories and intellectual backgrounds. These are the driving force behind research into sources, interpretations, and historical writings.The theories of consumption that developed in modern times are rooted in the crucial period at the end of the ancien régime around the seventeenth century, a period that marked the end of a consumer pattern that directly reflected the hierarchical division of classes through sumptuary laws. These laws regulated the quality and quantity of usable goods, especially clothing, on the basis of class, profession, and gender, indirectly reinforcing the social status quo, as Alan Hunt has shown. In fact, what was at issue here was ‘luxury’ rather than ‘consumption’, and luxury was usually condemned in religious and moral terms.It was Bernard Mandeville with The Fable of Bees (1714) who overtly contested the positions held at the time, suggesting that private vices – aspirations to luxury – were a seamless complement to public virtues – the development of commerce and the growth of communal wealth. This cast doubt on the fundamental link between parsimony, morality, and socioeconomic growth in nations throughout history. The eighteenth century saw protagonists becoming entrenched in one of two positions. One group continued to stigmatize luxury as a form of inequality – in The Spirit of the Laws (1748) Montesquieu condemned luxury in the political structure of a republic, where all citizens are called to work toward the common good, but accepted it under a monarchy, where it would symbolize the inevitable social gulf and encourage the development of trade. Rousseau wrote that only austerity was suitable for a virtuous republic, on the pattern of ancient Sparta. On the contrary, David Hume in his essay On Refinement of the Arts (1742) justified luxury in modern society as an engine for the economy, recognizing that its significance was very different in ancient societies, as shown by Christopher J. Berry in his book on the concept of luxury. In his work The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) Adam Smith assigns a particularly important role to the theory of consumption: the author restates the need to separate moral from economic judgments, emphasizing that individual egoism and the new market mechanisms could coexist with luxury and social inequality, damping down the ‘revolutionary’ effect that the spread of luxury seemed to be having in the societies of the time.Throughout the nineteenth century and on into the early twentieth century, the process of industrialization in Western societies produced many important effects, above all a focus on the economic and statistical aspects signaling a change in consumer patterns at all social levels. Alongside the references to consumption in the works of the most famous economists – David Ricardo, Alfred Marshall, Léon Walras, and finally Karl Marx, with his distinction between value of use and value of exchange of goods – we should spotlight two great scholars, Le Play and Halbwachs. Frédéric Le Play was a pioneer in research into family budgets, showing the contribution of statistical instruments to the growth of knowledge in this field, shifting the center of gravity of research from single individuals to families as a fundamental unit of consumption. In 1913 Maurice Halbwachs developed an influential theory that contested ‘Engel's law’, where family consumption increased in direct proportion to wealth (from basic consumption of goods like food to more sophisticated outlets for wealth like culture, well-being, and travel). By introducing elements of social and cultural analysis he showed that at equal income levels, cultural elements could radically alter consumption patterns – for example, a worker's family and a middle-class family could have a similar income but diverse consumption.At the same time, Werner Sombart's works, with their background in economy studies, exerted a great deal of influence. He saw luxury as one of the basic differences between the modern capitalist society and societies of the past. Thorstein Veblen was extremely influential in the United States: in his work The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899) in particular he analyzed overt displays of consumption by the new affluent classes as a symbolic banner deployed by the new rich to make a public statement of their wealth in a society where old distinctions of birth and class had definitively broken down. ‘Conspicuous consumption’ became one of the main methods of displaying social status, and came to form a specific feature in the profound economic and social transformation that was taking place in modern capitalist societies.Many of these theories, especially those with a critical intent, were taken up in the years to come by the analyses of the Frankfurt School, which played a crucial role in examining consumption throughout the mid-twentieth century, from the late 1930s to the 1960s and 1970s. Many works treated the new consumer world, with contributions from high-profile figures like Walter Benjamin, Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer, and, later, Herbert Marcuse. However, the work that perhaps had the greatest impact was Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944), where Adorno and Horckheimer, taking a typically Marxian analysis as their starting point, developed a hard-hitting critique of consumerism, seeing it as the tool of a new form of oppression that acted through the manipulation of desires at every level of society, exercising power in a new way. Everything became a commodity; everything was bought and sold. Culture no longer had a libertarian, critical function, it had been transformed into an industry, becoming a consumable in its turn. In his work The Society of the Spectacle (1967), Guy Debord produced a definition that met with great success, identifying the entertainment-consumption tandem as a key to reading contemporary society – from a negative stance, of course.Although they adopted a more concrete approach with a less negative thrust, theorists from the United States like John Kenneth Galbraith (The Affluent Society, 1958), Vance Packard, and David Riesman also highlighted the manipulative mechanisms involved in consumption in contemporary society, in this case linked above all to the activities of large corporations and the mass-media world. However, the late 1970s saw the development of a field of study on consumption that would lay the foundations for a different viewpoint. In particular the cultural studies tradition nurtured at Birmingham by Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall began to analyze the new youth subcultures that were often expressed through new forms of consumption. These highlighted broad areas of independence and choice among such consumers, regarded for the first time as autonomous subjects, not passive victims of political and commercial manipulation.Cultural developments in the 1980s led historians of consumption to cast their net even wider, taking in theoretical contributions emerging from the fields of semiotics, sociology, anthropology, and philosophy. One of the most influential thinkers was Roland Barthes, who spoke explicitly of ‘mythologies’ underlying even the most everyday acts of consumption. These acts became significant in themselves, and were rooted in complex historical contexts. Every object is made up not only of a material form, it is also charged with a ‘universe of meanings’ and deep cultural connotations that must be decoded. Every object is a sign of language. Jean Baudrillard studied above all the unreal dimension of the world of consumption, underscoring the proliferation of ‘simulacra’ created for commercial purposes. Drawing on reality as well as contents of the imagination, they eventually replace reality itself. The glamorous world of shopping and entertainment become our existential reference points. The work emanating from sociology departments also had a great impact, with Michel de Certeau and his analysis of the creation of social practices through everyday consumption, while anthropology also made important contributions. In this connection, the two main figures were Mary Douglas and Arjun Appadurai, who assigned a crucial role in communicating our identity to objects and material culture, given their ability to incorporate meanings. Pierre Bourdieu's notion of ‘habitus’, developed in relation to strategies of social differentiation based on consumption, had a great impact. Finally, work on social dynamics in contemporary society analyzed the creation of collective aggregations through shared consumption patterns, partly through the use of technical software.Show moreView chapterExplore bookRead full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780080970868621062Reference work2015, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (Second Edition)Emanuela ScarpelliniChapterPestalozzi, Johann Heinrich (1746–1827)2001, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral SciencesP. Korte2.2 From 1780 to 1799: Livelihood as an Independent WriterOut of the necessity of having to finance himself, Pestalozzi became a writer. In 1780 he published Abendstunde eines Einsiedlers whose theme is cultivating people: ‘Cultivating people towards the truth means cultivating their being and their nature towards a reassuring wisdom.’ Then he wrote the first part of Lienhard und Gertrud, which appeared in 1781. Lienhard und Gertrud is a pedagogical novel which its author broadened into a novelistic pedagogical text. The theme of the novel is the story of the education and cultivation of an entire village. With Lienhard und Gertrud, Pestalozzi wrote about a fictitious village which he called Bonnal in a novel showing both the development and the education of the characters. The subject of the novel is bound together by a kaleidoscope of multifaceted and fictitious stories of education, cultivation, and socialization.In the second (1783) and third (1785) books, it becomes clear how many individual fates have been embroiled in the deplorable state of affairs in Bonnal for many years, and that it is thereby not only a question of individual error, but at the same time of failings which lie more deeply in the political structure. Only in the fourth book (1787) does it become possible to continue telling the story of Bonnal and to organize it structurally as a story of reform, with, of course, further novelistic twists and turns and subplots. The village as the scene of the action is increasingly abandoned. Paragraph by paragraph Pestalozzi outlines his ideas for new legislation, the distribution of land, jurisdiction, and the culture of debate and justice. The novel is therefore increasingly interrupted on the level of action and plot, becomes more difficult to read, and thus loses its original novelistic character. The literary code transforms into a politically discursive text. Lienhard und Gertrud became Pestalozzi's greatest literary success. Pestalozzi was soon to become known far beyond the Swiss borders, first of all not as a pedagog, but as a writer. The novel brought him the title of Honorary Citizen during the French Revolution.In Gesetzgebung und Kindermord (written in 1780 and printed in 1783), Pestalozzi declared the prevailing legal practice throughout Europe of executing child-murderesses—mostly after extreme humiliation and torture—as inhuman. He mounted an emotive defence of a large number of child-murderesses, whom he viewed as innocent. To him, poor girls and women had the fundamental right to sexuality and marriage, to their children, to protection and support, and to recognition and help. The work was a plea against capital punishment.In 1782, Pestalozzi published Christoph und Else, a novel of instruction, even a ‘novel’ for the novel Lienhard und Gertrud. It was to be used as a guide to how adults should read Lienhard und Gertrud. A peasant family talk together over 30 evenings about the plot, the theme, and the constellation of characters in Lienhard und Gertrud. On 26 August 1792, Pestalozzi was appointed an Honorary French Citizen and never renounced the honorary title in spite of all the criticism of the Terror, an action which aroused suspicion in conservative circles. The outcome of Pestalozzi's examination of the revolution was the work Ja oder Nein? (1793) in which he made the Ancien Régime responsible for the devastating outrages in Europe and thus justified the revolution, though at the same time he sharply denounced the revolutionary Terror.In 1797, Pestalozzi's main philosophical work Meine Nachforschungen über den Gang der Natur in der Entwicklung des Menschengeschlechts appeared. The initial question was ‘What am I, and what is mankind?’ Pestalozzi expounded a natural state, a social state, and a moral state of humanity, and went on to discuss the individual human being as a ‘work of himself,’ a ‘work of nature,’ and a ‘work of morality.’In 1798, the revolution also reached Switzerland. For a short time, a Helvetic Republic was established. Pestalozzi became the editor of the ‘Helvetisches Volksblatt’—the publication organ of the new Helvetic government—and at first worked on behalf of the government. He wrote texts, appeals, and pamphlets, as well as Abhandlung über die Natur des Helvetischen Zehnden. Whereas the typical pamphlets on both sides at the time of the revolution constituted obvious works of political agitation in favor of one side or the other, Pestalozzi was a mediator who urged the often very hostile opposing groups towards agreement. He became a soother of passions in his pamphlets. KorteChapterThird World2015, International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (Second Edition)Maxwell OwusuThe Origin of the Term and Its Varied MeaningsThe term Third World (Le Tier Monde) is of French origin. It was first used in France in the early 1950s by a number of French writers like Alfred Sauvy (politician, economist who is credited with coining the term in 1952) and Claude Boudel in the context of apparently increasing polarization of the international system into rival blocs. The term conveys a conscious echo of the older concept of le tiers état that is, the third estate (the common people, the poor and underprivileged) of the prerevolutionary ancien régime. Some claim that it was Frantz Fanon, a black French Caribbean writer and psychiatrist from Martinique (author of The Wretched of the Earth, 1963) who first used the term to refer to the poor decolonized and decolonizing societies and territories of Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Educated in France, Fanon was a political activist who worked in Algeria, supported the Algerian nationalist struggle for independence from French occupation in the 1950s, and developed revolutionary theories for the decolonization of Africa. A weasel word, the term Third World has been used in several related senses, substituting for or succeeding other terms used by Europeans to refer to non-European peoples and cultures: aboriginal, indigenous savage, barbarous, traditional, (primitive, tribal, peasant) native, Indian, Mohammedan, pagan, precapitalist, preindustrial, preliterate, non-Western, nonwhite, premodern, and black. Such terms have been used sometimes with deliberate contempt and condescension, with pejorative connotations, or even racist overtones.These terms have also been adopted by the educated, more privileged urban dwellers in the Third World itself.Third World has also been employed as a shorthand euphemism for the social condition or plight of the very poor or powerless or underdeveloped society anywhere in the world, including the First and Second Worlds, even though a vast majority of the people fitting the description live in the Third World. In this sense, the phrase America's Third World refers to America's rural and urban poor: the black underclass, Native Americans, and rural whites in Appalachia. In a similar usage, the former Soviet Union was once described by the Times of London as having a Third World economy with First World weapons. South Africa is described as a First World society in which the Third World is ever present.The term Third World has also been extended to the poorer Eastern European countries whose economies were subjected to the needs of and exploited by Northern Europe in the early modern period. In everyday use, the term has thus acquired loose, but frequently negative, social, cultural, political, economic, ideological, and racial meanings, often with a fine disregard for geography. From 1945 to 1989 a capitalist block (First World) led by the United States and a communist one (Second World) led by the Soviet Union fought a Cold War that ended with the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. In the Cold War context, the Third World consisted mostly of newly decolonized, uncommitted countries not aligned diplomatically with either the capitalist world or the communist world.
